utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I've asked you about the substance of your records, how many statements there are, what form the statements are in, and whether they were taken under oath, and thus far you have not answered that. You keep going around the issue. So tell me if you are basing your findings on some body of documents, what body of documents are those so I can ask to see them so that I can do my cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: So, as I said before and I shall now repeat, we do not take any statements under oath. We collect requests submitted by families who are looking for their missing relatives. Our task boils down to this: Track down any missing persons with no further involvement in the sense of prosecuting those potentially responsible for these disappearances. That is down to the public Prosecutor, the police and everyone else who then joins in at the exhumation stage. But we take no statements under oath. We collect and receive requests from families and these are normally very specific. Personal details, circumstances, clothes that a person was wearing when they went missing, what was the last time they were seen --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt, sir. All these things that you have been reciting, where is that in your statement, where is that in your report? Where are descriptions of what people were wearing when they left, dates of when they disappeared? None of that is in your report. What is in your report is the stuff I'm asking about that says according to statements, the survivors were executed and burnt at two locations in the town of Visegrad itself. And you have said on the record, you are relying upon evidence, records. I want to know what evidence, what records you are relying upon in giving this testimony.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I'm relying on statements made by the relatives of victims. In the case of Pionirska Street, I'm relying on the statement of a surviving victim, among others.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There, now we've gone around full circuit to statements. Again I ask you: These statements that you are relying upon, are they sworn statements? What form are these statements? And how many of them are there?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: No statements were taken that involve this specific statement that I made for this trial. No statements, no special statements were taken from survivors or witnesses. I simply deduced a number of things based on evidence available to the Institute for Missing Persons. I didn't do this specifically for the purposes of this trial, in the sense of interviewing any victims. I extrapolated all of my conclusions based on records that are available to the Institute for Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, move on to another point now. MR.IVETIC: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In gathering information from sources for your report, am I correct that you did -- that you did not consider figures or statistics that were considered unreliable such as those from "enemy" missing persons commissions?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right. As I have pointed out already, these annexes contain the identities of both Bosniak and Muslim and Croat persons. I am not sure if you should warrant any further explanation on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: In your 2003 sworn statement, you identified who the enemy is to you as being groups related to the Serb authorities in the Republika Srpska, Croat authorities in Herceg Bosnia and Muslim authorities allied with Fikret Avdic, as well as those relating to the JNA. Do you stand by those qualifications as to whom you consider your enemies to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There's a reference to 2003 sworn statement. If we could have a more detailed reference to the exact statement and date. MR.IVETIC: Absolutely, Your Honour. If we could pull it up on the e-court it's 0294-1612, the ERN number. I believe it's an ICTY statement taken by this Office of the Prosecutor in the year 2003 of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number as well. MR.IVETIC: Yes. ERN number 0294-1612. That's the first page, do you need the whole range?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, I guess, do you recall giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2003?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I gave several statements. This is the fourth time that I'm giving evidence before this Tribunal. I sometimes provided some statements as well. But I can't possibly imagine a reason to believe that what you are suggesting to me is untrue. I provided several statements over the years, but perhaps I might even try to answer your question. In the period between --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: In the period between 1992 and the end of the war, I was an official of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The only legal government in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Needless to say, you mentioned on some -- you mentioned some forces and I described those between 1992 and 1995 as enemy forces, but from the point of view of the BH government that is a well-known fact. So between 1992 and 1995 those forces were, from our perspective, enemy forces. Enemy in relation to the government in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you still consider persons who are part of the police or military in Republika Srpska or in the Croatian Herceg-Bosnia or in the Avdic Western Bosnia to be enemies; and if not, when did you stop considering them enemies?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Probably when the war ended, when peace came again, the hostilities ceased, right? And once the peace agreement or peace accords in Dayton were signed, we stopped being enemies because peace was now back. As of the spring or summer of 1996, there has been cooperation between forces that up until then during the war had been clashing or had been hostile parties. But if you are asking me personally, even during the war itself, I worked with the enemies, I was the head of the Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War and one of my basic missions was to negotiate with the enemy in order to get people released from camps and prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say you still harbour a certain sort of animosity towards the enemy and acts that the enemy committed?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure who you are defining as my potential enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In your statement you define who the enemy is and I've read that to you. Do you still consider -- do you hold animosity towards those former enemies still for events that occurred during the war?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say that I harbour any feelings at all. If you are trying to get me to say that I'm harbouring hostile feelings, I have to say that that wasn't even the case during the war. During the war, we were on the opposite sides and there's no need for you to harbour any feelings. Your enemy is your enemy. You fight your enemy for as long as there are hostility, but if you ask me if I harboured any hostile feelings --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: One microphone at a time, please. We can't hear the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Interpreter is pleading again. You are overlapping. Please observe a pause between question and answer. MR.IVETIC:

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you have an occasion to review the indictment in this case against Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I think not. I think I saw bits of it over the internet, but I don't think I've ever seen the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the specific crimes or killings in Visegrad that you have set forth in your report in pages 7 onward, how were those selected to be presented? Did the Prosecution tell you what aspects to cover in your report? How was the coverage of your report selected?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: On page 7, there are no aspects. All I was saying is this: Based on my research, this or that was the difference between Visegrad municipality and Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole. I also observed that Visegrad municipality, in some cases, had a far larger number of victims from some particularly vulnerable population groups such as children, women or elderly persons. This is not something that someone required me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the statistical parts, sir. I'm talking specifically here, you talk about events in Pionirska and Bikavac. Then you go on to talk about Slap, you go on to talk about an execution and you mention someone's name there. You talk about, later on, again identifying various victims from Bikavac and Pionirska. How was that coverage selected in your report?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And Your Honours, I'd like to ask for the previous exhibit, the 2003 statement to be introduced into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D77, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what I did boils down to this: I wanted to point out in my statement certain peculiarities of Visegrad municipality in relation to other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, one of these peculiarities is the conspicuously large number of missing children, women, and people over 70 years of age. Another peculiarity, and this is reflected in my statement, is the number of missing persons who were found in Visegrad lies under the 50 percent mark as opposed to that in the other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then I go on to state in my conclusion why that is so. Because statements by survivors provide accounts of bodies being thrown into the River Drina, bodies being burned leaving no remains or traces. This is a peculiarity, it's particularly prominent in Visegrad. This is not the only peculiarity, but it appears in a particularly emphatic or dramatic form in Visegrad municipality. But I was not specifically requested to do this. What I was specifically requested to do is to update information in relation to the Vasiljevic case which I did in my tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was it your understanding and do you consider it your work product, this statement, to be your expert report on the research you did and the conclusions you drew? Was that your assignment?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Again, this is not research. This is not scientific methodology. All this is is an analysis based on such information as was contained in our records on missing persons. This is not research. If I had conducted research, being no expert or researcher myself, I would have enlisted somebody else 's assistance. If I had decided to take that course of action, as I say. On the other hand, I'm a person who has been dealing with this sort of problem for the last 16 years. I have certain information, I have certain knowledge on such issues as missing persons or victim identification. I cannot, however, consider myself an expert in any of these fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, what portion of this statement, which is your testimony, is based on your eyewitness knowledge?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: So, if you go to page 3, we are talking about 67 locations that had been processed where the mortal remains of victims had been found. I did go to some of these 67 locations so I have direct knowledge, not of how the victims were killed, but rather, of how they were exhumed at these locations. And then of course everything else that followed the exhumations. PMs, bodies being identified and then bodies being delivered back to their families. I'm now at page 4. I don't, however, have any direct knowledge of Pionirska Street or whatever occurred there. My knowledge is based on accounts provided by family members who were looking for their own kin who had gone missing. And in the case of Pionirska Street, on the account of a witness who had survived Pionirska Street. Bikavac, again, I have no direct knowledge of Bikavac. Zepa, Slap 1, 125 victims; Slap 2, seven victims. I was directly involved in the exhumation work from day one at this specific location. The same can be said of this pit in the village of Paklenik where 73 victims were found, some of them from Visegrad. Again, my knowledge is due to a surviving victim, a survivor who took us to this location after the war. He pointed out to us the exact spot where the killing took place and where the remains or the bodies were thrown into a natural pit that was 35 or 37 metres deep. And then the last grave site, page 4, the Kurtalici grave site, again, I went there myself when the grave site was discovered and when the exhumation took place and bodies were dug up and extracted from the pit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, am I right in saying that the Prosecution is relying on this evidence to prove certain aspects of the indictment? For example, the widespread character of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that in the case of where the report speaks to deaths, we would need to be sure that the report itself is reliable in that regard. Of course he may have other evidence in relation to those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the report, I believe this witness is in the course of testifying of his own personal knowledge relating to the mass number of grave sites, both mass grave sites and individual grave sites that were present in and around the Visegrad municipality. This witness has personal knowledge of those grave sites and he is testifying accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic. MR.IVETIC: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just briefly on exhumations, sir. Am I correct that you don't have any formal training as a forensic pathologist as a forensic crime scene evidence gatherer or any other scientific forensic expertise, that you were there as a layperson making observations?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: So, I do have some basic -- I don't think I could call it education or training, but I do have some basic knowledge because all of us who were involved in these procedures, six or seven years ago, had to go through some sort of abbreviated training in relation to these matters. Nevertheless, you are quite right, I have no expert knowledge or qualifications as far as the forensic science is concerned, nor would I dare go too far in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as the work done by your commission is concerned, am I correct that during some period your commission was responsible for issuing certificates on missing and dead persons which enabled families to receive financial benefits?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: This is something that certified the fact that a person had gone missing. This is a certificate that is used to certify that a certain person was identified as missing with the institute. This is not a death certificate, this is not a certificate that would allow a family to inherit something from this missing person in terms of being a relative, marriage or perhaps something to do with custody over children. This certificate is called Certificate on Missing Persons, and families used this certificate under the Federation law to obtain certain financial compensation pursuant to the fact that they had one, two or more family members who had at some point gone missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with respect to the forensic examination that you witnessed at the Pionirska and Bikavac sites, and in your report you state that no mortal remains were found at those locations and you give the conclusion that, therefore, the mortal remains were taken to secondary sites. Isn't it also true that another possible conclusion based upon the forensic evidence at the site was that those crimes in fact did not occur?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Theoretically, yes. However, that would imply that all those, and we are talking about hundreds of people or more, who came to the institute to report one of their own as missing were lying. All those who came and who said my father, my mother, my child, my brother, my sister went missing in what occurred on the 14th of June at Pionirska Street. So this would imply, in other words, that all those people were lying, and this is something that I find difficult to believe. I wasn't there myself on the 14th of June. Obviously I can't tell you whether it happened or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me that it's a separate issue. Someone saying that a loved one is missing is a separate issue from affirmatively stating that a loved one perished in a particular incident? Would you not agree with that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I need to go back to what I said before. They submit to us a request to track someone down. The families normally state the circumstances of disappearance and when they state that normally they include information like that. My folks were over at the house on Pionirska Street and they were killed or burnt alive there, or another person comes up and says, I saw someone chuck someone else into the Drina River, and then a surviving witness, for example, says, I went over to the Paklenik pit and I know that people had been shot there because I am survivor. Forensic technicians, for example, go to the pit in Paklenik and they find dozens of empty cartridges, again, indicating something that they base their own conclusions on. I was the head of the Committee for Missing Persons and I am into their conclusions. I believe they can draw their own conclusions but I drew mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I guess, sir, that I'm at loss because I don't have these hundreds of statements from victims, families that you have mentioned. I've asked you over half an hour ago how many statements you had and you didn't answer me then, you've answered me now. These hundreds of statements, did your organisation take any steps to verify the information given by relatives in the same?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: So, the only thing we could verify was the location at which a missing person was buried. Now 13 years after the war, it's perfectly clear that all those and most of those that are listed as missing are no longer alive. The institute has more than 13.000 anti-mortem reports in its possession. It is a special form running into 16 pages. I can't say that specifically because I didn't write this statement based on some statements but, rather, based on the records that we have. The records that are in our electronic database.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, how much longer will you be? MR.IVETIC: I am much shorter. I was, in fact, going to inquire if it would be possible just to introduce -- we have a sworn statement from an individual Jasmin Odobasic, that the Office of the Prosecutor disclosed to us yesterday, that makes certain allegations as to the covering up of certain things by various persons, and I would -- in lieu of asking and going through those with the witness, I would tender them. If the Prosecution has anything in redirect, they are free to comment on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would object to this as a form of introducing this evidence, this statement. It's not this witness's statement. I do know that the witness is -- from discussing it with him yesterday when this matter came up, that he would be able to address these issues in closed session if the -- if counsel would like to put it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, it's a question of time. I've been investigating whether it would be possible first for us to meet tomorrow morning to conclude this witness's evidence. And so far what I've heard is, the legal officer will now tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, well, with the information that I have gathered, I'm able to say that there is a courtroom available tomorrow morning. The problem is that everyone has gone home. It's dark outside, in case you don't know, and so we are not able to ascertain the availability of the personnel and staff that we need, but the court deputy says that she will be in a position to let us know relatively early in the morning and so I would say 10.30. We would resume at 10.30 unless you are otherwise advised. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may assist, I will have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I can give all my time to Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, in that case we might be able to finish with the indulgence of the interpreters. Mr. Ivetic, how much longer? MR.IVETIC: I would anticipate five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, may I ask for the indulgence of the interpreters for another 10, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are indebted to you. MR.IVETIC: And you have my thanks as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, before we --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I understand we need to be in closed session now. And, Your Honours, and then we should probably redact prior references, I was not advised of any --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Prosecution has no objection to the prior references just whatever further explanation comes from those questions, if we could handle them in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
